source.version: Journal version of record: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 4 (2025) 100140; received 30 December 2024, revised 12 March 2025, accepted and available online 19 March 2025 (p. 1). Elsevier typeset PDF, CC BY-NC-ND.
source.title_on_document: If ChatGPT can do it, where is my creativity? generative AI boosts performance but diminishes experience in creative writing

supplement.where: Appendix A. Supplementary data, online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2025.100140 (p. 13)
supplement.holds: SI Table 1 (demographics by group, likely the arm sizes), SI Table 2 (ICC among raters), SI Table 3 (performance regressions of frequency, flexibility, inaccuracy, unclarity and writing time on condition, within each group and across groups: coefficients and SEs), SI Table 4 (HAI dyad analysis), SI Table 5 (group-level creativity), SI Table 6 (perception regressions). The pooled across-group treatment effects on the creativity outcomes appear only in SI Table 3; the main text prints just three nonsignificant per-group coefficients and figures.

paper_design_summary: 225 UK university students recruited on Prolific (after 43 attention-check exclusions) were randomly assigned, between subjects, to write a short piece (about 100 words, 10 minutes) describing as many uses as possible for a printer that can print anything in 2097, either required to use ChatGPT or forbidden from using it. Participants were first labelled into four groups by native English speaker status and prior ChatGPT experience, with balance across conditions. Outputs were scored for fluency (number of uses) and flexibility (number of conceptual domains) by GPT-4o few-shot prompting validated against three human raters, and for grammar errors and clarity suggestions with Grammarly; pre/post perception surveys were also collected.

studies.label: Online experiment: printer-uses creative writing task with vs without ChatGPT

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition: AI group (explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the task) vs control (forbidden from using ChatGPT). Assignment balanced across four groups defined by English proficiency and prior ChatGPT experience.
assignment.quote: the experiment used a between-subjects design to randomly assign participants into one of two treatment conditions: the control condition (these participants were forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task) and the experimental condition or 'AI group'
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 2.2 Design; also p. 4, Fig. 1 caption ('we used a between-subjects design to randomly assign all participants to one of the two experimental conditions (Control vs. AI)')
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 4, Section 2.1 ('Methods, hypotheses and analyses of the study were pre-registered online at Open Science Frame'); pp. 12-13, Pre-registration section, https://osf.io/dt5up

arms.name: AI
arms.description: Participants explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the writing task; reported their ChatGPT usage afterwards.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Participants forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task; reported any tool usage afterwards (90 percent reported using no digital tools, p. 6).

participants.exclusions: A total of 266 participants completed the study; 43 who failed the attention check were excluded, 'leaving a final sample of 225' (p. 4). Note 266 - 43 = 223, not 225; the four group counts (58 + 60 + 54 + 53) sum to 225 (p. 4). Whether exclusions happened before or after assignment is not stated. Arm sizes are not given in the main text (possibly in SI Table 1). Some t-tests report df of 221 and 220 (p. 8).
participants.who: Current students at a university in the United Kingdom recruited via Prolific; mean age 29.07 (SD 8.59); 60 percent undergraduates, 31 percent postgraduates. Four groups: non-native inexperienced n = 58, native inexperienced n = 60, non-native experienced n = 54, native experienced n = 53.
participants.quote: A total of 266 participants completed the study, all current students studying at a university in the United Kingdom. ... Forty-three people who failed the attention check were excluded from further analysis, leaving a final sample of 225.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1 Participants and Section 2.2 Design

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT (model version used by participants not stated). GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo were used only by the researchers to score outputs.
ai_tool.how_used: AI-arm participants were required to use ChatGPT freely for the task. Self-reports: 27 percent relied entirely on ChatGPT, 47 percent made minor or major changes to AI output, 21 percent used their own prompts or a feedback loop, 5 percent unclassified (p. 6, Section 3.2.2).

task.description: Short written piece (approx. 100 words) describing as many unique uses as possible for a hypothetical 'printer that can print anything in 2097', while minimising grammar errors and maximising clarity. The paper calls it a creative writing task; it is scored as an unusual-uses divergent-thinking test.

outcomes.name: Frequency (fluency): number of different uses of the printer
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Uses counted by LLM few-shot prompting (GPT4o and GPT4 Turbo, temperature 0). Validation on 40 random responses (5 per group x condition) annotated by three blinded human raters from the research team: average human ICC 0.81; human average vs GPT-4o ICC 0.93 for frequency (p. 5).

contrasts.reported: Main text: pooled across groups AI participants had 'higher frequency and flexibility of creativity' (p. 6); pooled regression only in SI Table 3. Fig. 2 shows per-group means with 95% CIs (no numbers printed). Group 2 (native, inexperienced) nonsignificant: b = 0.91, SE = 2.30, p = .69. Group 4 (native, experienced): no significant difference in frequency (no numbers printed). Fig. 3 shows means by 21 demographic subgroups.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2 and Fig. 2; p. 7, Fig. 3; SI Table 3 (not in this PDF)

outcomes.name: Flexibility: number of unique conceptual domains represented by the uses
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Domains counted by LLM few-shot prompting (GPT4o and GPT4 Turbo, temperature 0). Human average vs GPT-4o ICC 0.83 for flexibility; average human inter-rater ICC 0.81 (p. 5). The paper describes flexibility as 'variety/quality of ideas'.

contrasts.reported: Main text: pooled across groups AI participants had higher flexibility (p. 6); regressions only in SI Table 3. Fig. 2 shows per-group means with 95% CIs (no numbers printed); Group 4 (native, experienced) no significant difference in flexibility (p. 6). Fig. 3 by demographic subgroups.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2 and Fig. 2; p. 7, Fig. 3; SI Table 3 (not in this PDF)

outcomes.name: Group-level creativity: frequency and flexibility scores for the pooled set of each condition (Fig. 5, Grp 9 'Task Treatment')
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Group-level frequency and flexibility for 'collections of participants that share a characteristic or condition' (p. 7). How the group-level score is computed (sum of individual counts or count of distinct uses/domains in the pooled set) is not described in the main text; SI Table 5 may say. The paper interprets it as diversity of ideas (Section 4.2.3, p. 10).

contrasts.reported: Text: 'people using ChatGPT outperform the Control group in both Flexibility (635 vs. 552) and Frequency (442 vs. 313)' (p. 7). Fig. 5 (p. 9) prints Grp 9 values as 313 (Control) vs 442 (AI) in the panel labelled Flexibility and 552 (Control) vs 635 (AI) in the panel labelled Frequency, i.e. the text swaps the labels relative to the figure. Exceptions for frequency: Grp 1 non-native inexperienced 140 (AI) vs 193 (Control); Grp 7 inexperienced 312 (AI) vs 344 (Control). No test statistics.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 3.2.3; p. 9, Fig. 5; SI Table 5 (not in this PDF)

diversity_detail.metric: Group-level frequency (uses) and flexibility (conceptual domains) per condition; computation not described
diversity_detail.computed_over: All outputs within a condition (or within a condition x subgroup cell), pooled; exact aggregation not stated
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported; single number per set, no test
diversity_detail.notes: Fig. 5 caption also swaps the colour legend in words ('red colour indicating using ChatGPT (the 'Control' condition)'), while the figure legend shows blue = AI, red = Control.

outcomes.name: Inaccuracy: number of grammar mistakes detected by Grammarly
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of spelling, grammar and punctuation mistakes flagged by Grammarly; lower is better (writing quality, not creativity).

contrasts.reported: AI participants had 'less inaccuracy and unclarity from their writing' (p. 6). Fig. 2 per-group means with 95% CIs; Group 4 no significant difference in correctness. Regressions in SI Table 3.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2 and Fig. 2; SI Table 3 (not in this PDF)

outcomes.name: Unclarity: number of Grammarly suggestions on word choice, sentence structure and tone
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of Grammarly clarity suggestions; lower is better (writing quality, not creativity).

contrasts.reported: Overall AI lower unclarity (p. 6). Nonsignificant in Group 2: b = -1.30, SE = 1.90, p = .51; Group 3: b = -2.30, SE = 1.50, p = .14; Group 4 no significant difference. Regressions in SI Table 3.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2 and Fig. 2; SI Table 3 (not in this PDF)

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned between subjects to use ChatGPT or not (p. 5; Fig. 1, p. 4); 225 people analyzed after attention-check exclusions (p. 4), well above 50 though the 266 - 43 arithmetic gives 223; fluency and flexibility are counted on the written output by GPT-4o validated against human raters (p. 5). Arm sizes and pooled effect statistics sit in the online SI.

one_line_finding: Students required to use ChatGPT listed more printer uses (fluency) and more conceptual domains (flexibility) than students forbidden from it, with nonsignificant differences among native English speakers (Group 2 frequency b = 0.91, SE = 2.30; Group 4 no significant creativity difference); pooled estimates are only in SI Table 3 and the main text shows them in Fig. 2 (p. 6).
open_questions: Arm sizes (AI vs Control) are not stated in the main text; check SI Table 1.
Sample arithmetic: 266 completed minus 43 excluded = 223, but the paper reports a final sample of 225 and group counts summing to 225 (p. 4); t-tests report df 221 and 220 (p. 8).
Pooled across-group treatment effects (coefficients, SEs) for frequency and flexibility appear only in SI Table 3, which is not in this PDF.

Group-level creativity (Fig. 5): the aggregation method is not described, so it is unclear whether it is a set-level diversity measure (distinct uses/domains across people) or a sum of individual counts. The text on p. 7 swaps the Flexibility and Frequency values relative to the Fig. 5 panels (p. 9).
Attention-check exclusions: timing relative to assignment not stated; no intention-to-treat analysis reported.
Outputs were scored by GPT-4o/GPT-4 Turbo; whether raters (human or LLM) could detect condition is a concern for AI-written text, though the 40-response human validation was blinded.
notes: Only one study. Writing time (shorter in the AI arm) is a process measure, not scored on the output, and is omitted from outcomes. Perception outcomes (value, enjoyment, difficulty, effort, trust, moral acceptance) are self-reported pre/post changes and omitted from outcomes. The HAI dyad analysis (Fig. 4, p. 8) splits the AI arm by self-reported usage type, which is not randomized. The candidate record's 'experiment_assignment_unclear' is resolved: the paper states random assignment between subjects (p. 5). The sentence on p. 4 that participants were 'randomly selected based on their English proficiency and prior experience with ChatGPT' describes the four-group stratification for balance across conditions.
